lesson.title: Chasing the Slope Under a Square Root
lesson.summary: The derivative of a root function falls right out of the power rule once you rewrite the root as a fractional exponent, and the limit definition confirms the same answer from scratch.
lesson.body:
A square root looks nothing like a polynomial, so it is tempting to think it needs its own separate differentiation trick. It does not. The key move, which you already met when you learned about fractional exponents, is to rewrite every root as a power: sqrt(x) is x^(1/2), the cube root of x is x^(1/3), and in general the nth root of x is x^(1/n). Once a root is written this way, the ordinary power rule, which says d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1), applies without any modification. The exponent just happens to be a fraction instead of a whole number.

Applying the power rule to x^(1/2) gives d/dx x^(1/2) = (1/2) x^(1/2 - 1) = (1/2) x^(-1/2). Rewriting the negative exponent as a fraction, x^(-1/2) = 1/x^(1/2) = 1/sqrt(x), so d/dx sqrt(x) = 1/(2 sqrt(x)). Notice what happened to the exponent: it dropped by exactly 1, from 1/2 to negative 1/2, exactly as the power rule demands, and the coefficient 1/2 came along for the ride. This is not a special rule for roots at all, it is the same power rule you already trust, just with fractions instead of integers.

It is worth checking that this answer is not a coincidence of the power rule but something the limit definition of the derivative also produces, since that definition is the actual meaning of a slope. Start with d/dx sqrt(x) = lim(h to 0) [sqrt(x+h) - sqrt(x)] / h. Direct substitution gives 0/0, so multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate sqrt(x+h) + sqrt(x). The numerator becomes (x+h) - x = h, so the quotient simplifies to h / [h(sqrt(x+h) + sqrt(x))], and the h cancels to leave 1 / [sqrt(x+h) + sqrt(x)]. Letting h go to 0 now causes no trouble, and the limit is 1 / [sqrt(x) + sqrt(x)] = 1/(2 sqrt(x)), matching the power rule answer exactly.

For a concrete check, take f(x) = sqrt(x) at x = 4. The formula gives f'(4) = 1/(2 sqrt(4)) = 1/(2*2) = 1/4. A quick numerical test confirms this: f(4.01) = sqrt(4.01), which is approximately 2.0025, so the difference quotient [f(4.01) - f(4)] / 0.01 is about (2.0025 - 2)/0.01 = 0.25, right in line with 1/4. The slope of the square root curve is fairly gentle near x = 4, and it gets even gentler as x grows, since 1/(2 sqrt(x)) shrinks toward 0.

The same reasoning handles any root. For the cube root, f(x) = x^(1/3), the power rule gives f'(x) = (1/3) x^(-2/3). At x = 8, where the cube root is 2, this evaluates to (1/3) * 8^(-2/3) = (1/3) * (1/4) = 1/12, since 8^(2/3) = (8^(1/3))^2 = 2^2 = 4. One caution worth flagging: the derivative formula 1/(2 sqrt(x)) blows up as x approaches 0, which matches the visual fact that the square root graph has a vertical tangent line at the origin, an infinitely steep slope where the ordinary rules of smooth curves briefly break down.

The fractional exponent view also handles a root sitting in a denominator without any extra work. Since 1/sqrt(x) equals x^(-1/2), the power rule gives d/dx x^(-1/2) = (-1/2) x^(-3/2) = -1/(2 x^(3/2)). No separate rule is needed for roots in denominators, because rewriting as a fractional, possibly negative, exponent absorbs that case automatically into the same power rule pattern. This habit, always rewriting a root as a fractional exponent before differentiating, is the single most useful takeaway here, and it is exactly what will let the chain rule later extend smoothly to roots wrapped around more complicated inner expressions instead of plain x.
